Homora finds the devices on your home network, checks your setup for common security problems, and shows where your Wi-Fi signal is strong or weak.

resources.string: Tap a device and choose \"This is mine\". Anything left unmarked deserves a closer look.
Someone shouldn\'t be on your Wi-Fi?

Android doesn\'t let apps see other devices\' hardware (MAC) addresses, and many devices don\'t announce a name. Phones also use a private, random address on Wi-Fi, so even your router may list them as unknown. An unknown device is usually something you own.
Unplug or switch off your devices one at a time. Homora checks every few seconds and tells you when this one disappears.

string-array.name: f_wifi_open_steps
string-array.item: Open your router\'s settings. The address and admin password are usually on a sticker on the router.
Find Wi-Fi or Wireless security.
Choose WPA2 or WPA3 and set a long password.
Reconnect your devices with the new password.

resources.string: Your Wi-Fi uses WEP, which is broken
WEP passwords can be cracked in minutes with free tools, so it protects almost nothing.

string-array.name: f_wifi_wep_steps
string-array.item: Open your router\'s settings and find Wi-Fi or Wireless security.
Switch to WPA2 or WPA3 and set a long password.
If your router only offers WEP, it is too old to be safe and should be replaced.

resources.string: Your Wi-Fi uses old WPA security
The original WPA (TKIP) has known weaknesses and also slows your Wi-Fi down.

string-array.name: f_wifi_old_wpa_steps
string-array.item: Open your router\'s settings and find Wi-Fi or Wireless security.
Choose WPA2 (AES) or WPA2/WPA3.
Reconnect any device that drops off afterwards.

resources.string: WPS lets devices join with a button or an 8-digit PIN. On many routers the PIN can be guessed, letting someone join without your password.

string-array.name: f_wps_on_steps
string-array.item: Open your router\'s settings and find the Wi-Fi or Wireless section.
Turn WPS off.
You can still add devices by typing the Wi-Fi password.

resources.string: UPnP lets any device on your network open ports in your router to the internet without asking you. Malware on one device can use it to expose others.

string-array.name: f_upnp_on_steps
string-array.item: Open your router\'s settings and look under Advanced, NAT or Forwarding.
Turn UPnP off.
If a game console or app stops working, set up a port forward for just that device instead.

resources.string: Telnet is an old, unencrypted remote login. The Mirai botnet took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers by logging in over Telnet with default passwords.

string-array.name: f_telnet_open_steps
string-array.item: Update the device\'s firmware from its app or web page.
Turn off Telnet in its settings, if there is an option.
Change the device\'s default password.
If none of that is possible, consider replacing it or moving it to a guest network.

resources.string: FTP sends passwords and files unencrypted, so anyone on your Wi-Fi could read them.

string-array.name: f_ftp_open_steps
string-array.item: If you don\'t use FTP, turn it off in the device\'s settings.
If you do, switch to an encrypted option such as SFTP, and use a strong password.

resources.string: VNC lets someone see and control this device\'s screen. Many VNC setups have weak passwords or none.

string-array.name: f_vnc_open_steps
string-array.item: If you don\'t use screen sharing, turn it off.
If you do, set a strong password and keep the software updated.

resources.string: A camera video stream is reachable
This device offers a video stream (RTSP) on your network. If it still uses its default password, anyone on your Wi-Fi could watch it.

string-array.name: f_camera_stream_open_steps
string-array.item: Change the camera\'s default password in its app.
Update its firmware.
If you only watch through the app, turn RTSP off if the camera allows it.

resources.string: Your router\'s settings page uses plain HTTP, so the admin password travels unencrypted when you log in. Someone on your Wi-Fi could capture it.

string-array.name: f_router_admin_unencrypted_steps
string-array.item: Change the router\'s admin password from the default.
Turn on HTTPS for the settings page if your router offers it.
Only log in to the router from devices you trust.

string-array.name: lockout_steps
string-array.item: Log in to your router\'s settings. The address and admin password are usually on a sticker on the router.
Change the router\'s admin password. It is different from the Wi-Fi password.
Turn off WPS, so no one can rejoin with the button or PIN.
Change the Wi-Fi password. Every device is disconnected and has to rejoin with the new one.
Reconnect your own devices.
Scan again in Homora to check the unknown device is gone.

resources.string: If it keeps coming back, reset the router to factory settings and set it up again. Homora never disconnects devices itself; that\'s done from your router, so you stay in control.
Link rate is the radio\'s maximum, not your internet speed.

Too weak. Expect drop-outs; move the router closer or add a mesh point.
Weak. Fine for browsing, poor for video calls.
Good for video calls and streaming.

Check what might be getting in the way
Most smart plugs, bulbs and cameras only work on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Here is what might be getting in the way.
Your phone is on %1$s. Many setup apps need the phone on 2.4 GHz while you add the device. Move further from the router, or turn off 5 GHz for a few minutes.
Your phone is on 2.4 GHz, which is right for setting up smart devices.

Your router uses one Wi-Fi name for both 2.4 and 5 GHz. Some smart devices fail to join like this. In the router\'s settings, give 2.4 GHz its own name (look for \"band steering\" or \"smart connect\"), then connect the device to it.
Your 2.4 and 5 GHz networks have separate names. Good.

When sharing is on, Homora sends: scan duration and device counts (as ranges, like \"6–15\"), the types of problems found, which guides were opened or marked wrong, Wi-Fi meter use, and crash reports. Firebase adds an app-instance ID, your phone model and Android version. Homora never sends device names, IP or MAC addresses, Wi-Fi names, or your location.
